title: Lost in Translation: What Stakeholders Really Mean

body.text: If I could give myself one piece of advice at the start of my transition into business analysis, it would be this: don’t put away what support already taught you.
One thing those years taught me is that people rarely describe a problem in the language of the solution. And I believe this applies to stakeholders just as much as it applies to consumers.

A consumer does not need to understand how a product works internally. They know what they are trying to achieve, what is getting in their way, and what they expect to happen. In many ways, stakeholders are similar.
Their role is not necessarily to describe the system, define every edge case, or explain how a solution should be implemented. Very often, they speak in the language of desired outcomes:

“We need users to be able to do X.”
“Process Y should become faster.”
“We need more visibility in Z.”
The language of engineering is different. It has to be structured, precise, and unambiguous — detailed enough to build the right thing, rather than merely something that works.

And somewhere between those two languages sits the Business Analyst. Not just as a messenger or a translator, but as a localizer — someone who adapts the meaning, context, and intent of a request to make it work in another professional language.

Understanding what someone wants, exploring why they want it, identifying constraints and exceptions, challenging assumptions where necessary, and eventually turning that intent into something developers and engineers can work with.

In support, I learned to understand what people are actually trying to achieve. Today, in a different role, I keep coming back to the same question: what are we actually trying to achieve here, what’s the end result we care about?
Different customer. Different language. Same question.
